newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian shares and dollar seen rising - IBSA.
newsitem.headline: Australian shares and dollar seen rising - IBSA.

text.p: Australian economists see favourable conditions for further gains by the share market and for a stronger local dollar, according to a survey by the International Banks and Securities Association (IBSA).
"IBSA economists predict a steady outlook for Australian financial markets," IBSA executive director Robert Webster said in a statement released with the June survey.
The All Ordinaries Index has recently broken above 2700 for the first time, and economists said medium term fundamentals remain positive for the share market.
Citibank senior economist Annette Beacher said she saw "some consolidation around 2,800 as the markets take a breather".
"But (the) trend growth/low inflation environment is ideal for heading towards 3000," she said.
Expectations of another rate cut, and low capital market yields would also help the market.
"With the 10-year bond yield around seven percent and another cash rate cut in the pipeline, equity market conditions remain favourable," UBS chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
For the Australian dollar, in the near term speculation over lower interest rates will weigh on it, but economists said a stronger outlook for commodity prices should help the dollar.

"Some short term weakness may be evident, but we expect it to remain, on average, around those levels for some time," Simes said. Not all economists thought the rates issue would be resolved or overshadowed by commodities.
"The Australian dollar will remain under pressure until the uncertainty surrounding the next movement in interest rates is resolved," Tokai Australia Finance economist Joanne Rains said.
For local interest rates, another cut was possible, but the economy was also looking to be stronger through the year.
Macquarie Bank's Shields said rates should be steady around current levels, with a cut dependent on the growth outlook.
"Another rate cut is likely but by no means certain," Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton said, adding long yields would tend to drift up with those in the United States.
"The March quarter set a base for stronger growth this year, although weak consumer spending remains a risk," he said.
Inflation is generally seen remaining under control, with some downside in coming quarters.

"The headline inflation figure will fall to near zero year-over-year in the next few quarters, as the benefits of lower mortgage rates are reflected in index calculation," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ivan Colhoun said.

"The more important underlying inflation rate will be below two percent in each quarter," he said. The Reserve Bank of Australia aims to keep the underlying rate between two and three percent over a number of years.
However, there was some concern the weaker Australian dollar and a lift in economic growth could see it move towards the top of the RBA range by the middle of next year.
